37082a91c6:
This chapter has two halves of one idea: information a downstream step needs must not be lost or disguised on the way.

Part one follows an error from a failing tool, through a subagent, to a coordinator and into the final report. At each hop, it shows what gets destroyed when the error is flattened to a string.

Part two follows a finding through a long Claude Code session on a large repository. It shows why specifics decay into "typical patterns". Then it builds the scratchpad, subagent and checkpoint machinery that stops the decay.

Code is in Python and Java/Spring, with a companion folder of runnable offline examples.
670ca60f63:
In a coordinator and subagent system the coordinator knows only what the subagent returns, so an error must travel as structured data (failure type, what was attempted, partial results, alternatives, and an honest coverage statement) and an access failure must never be returned as an empty result.

In a long exploration session the model's memory of specific findings decays under volume and under compaction, so confirmed findings must be written to disk, verbose discovery must run in subagents, and each phase must end with an exported state that a fresh session can resume from.
d4d42e7e04:
Both halves are about the same failure. A fact exists somewhere in the system, and the component that needs it can't get it. Or it gets a distorted version and can't tell.

In 5.3, the lost fact is why something failed. In 5.4, it's what was already found. In both, the exam rewards the answer that moves the fact into an explicit, structured, durable place. It punishes the answers that hope the fact survives: retry harder, abort everything, use a bigger context window, compact more.
b8928fe8b6:
The official task statement for 5.3 lists these knowledge points, each taught below:

  • structured error context, including failure type, attempted query, partial results and alternative approaches;
  • the distinction between access failures (timeouts, which need a retry decision) and valid empty results (a successful query with no matches);
  • why generic error statuses hide valuable context;
  • why silently suppressing errors (returning an empty result as success) and terminating the whole workflow on a single failure are both anti-patterns;
  • local recovery inside subagents for transient failures, with only unresolvable errors propagated;
  • coverage annotations in the final output.

For 5.4:

  • context degradation in extended sessions (inconsistent answers, "typical patterns" in place of the specific classes found);
  • scratchpad files that persist key findings across context boundaries;
  • subagent delegation for verbose exploration;
  • summarising one phase before the next;
  • structured state exported for crash recovery;
  • /compact.
39f263ce76: Passing failure information from one component to another without losing its meaning is one of the oldest problems in distributed systems. Every generation re-learned the same lesson, and those lessons line up with what the exam asks. A telecom architect has seen most of them first-hand.
9351ecdf03:
In C, a failing call returned a code and a convention, usually -1 and errno. The dominant bug was the caller that never checked it.

Exceptions (CLU, Ada, C++, then Java in 1995) fixed that. They made failure impossible to ignore by accident. Then the industry discovered the second bug: catch (Exception e) {}, the swallowed exception, which turns a failure into silence. Java's checked exceptions were an argument about exactly this trade-off. Reviewers usually rank an empty catch block among the worst smells in a codebase.

The silent-suppression anti-pattern in this chapter is that same bug, carried into an agent system: except Exception: return [].
5a9cd2688e:
Telecom protocols encode the failure classification in the code itself, because the receiver has to act without a human.

SIP splits responses into classes. 4xx are client errors: the request is wrong, and retrying it unchanged won't help. 5xx are server errors: this server failed, but another may succeed. 6xx are global failures: no server will succeed.

Diameter result codes separate 2xxx success, 4xxx transient failures (try again later) and 5xxx permanent failures (do not retry).

A timeout at the transport layer is a different thing again. It doesn't say whether the peer processed the request. These systems have retry timers, fallback to a secondary peer, and explicit "no answer" handling.

The design question was never "did it fail". It was "what should the caller do next", and the code carries that answer. A failure_type plus retryable pair in an error payload is the same idea.
840851b35f:
Joe Armstrong's Erlang work (his 2003 thesis, built on the telephony switches at Ericsson) argued that a process shouldn't try to handle every error locally. It should fail visibly and let a supervisor decide what to do. The supervisor has the context to choose between restarting, retrying and escalating.

Michael Nygard's Release It! (2007) catalogued stability patterns for the other direction: how a caller protects itself from a failing callee. Timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fail fast.

Both traditions agree on two points that this chapter relies on. The failing component reports what happened. The component with the wider view decides the recovery. A subagent recovers what it can locally (a bounded retry, the Erlang analogue of a quick restart) and escalates the rest to the coordinator, which plays the supervisor.
832ecb6e92:
HTTP gave APIs a status code and left the body unspecified. So every service invented its own error JSON, usually {"error":"something went wrong"}.

RFC 7807 (2016), "Problem Details for HTTP APIs", defined a standard body with type, title, status, detail and instance, plus room for extension members. RFC 9457 (2023) obsoleted it with clarifications. Spring 6 added ProblemDetail for it. gRPC took a similar route, with a fixed set of status codes and rich error details.

The shape the exam wants for tool errors is a problem-details body with extension members for the things an agent can act on: retryable, attempted_query, partial_results, alternatives.
bc928be826:
Garcia-Molina and Salem's sagas (1987) tackled long-running transactions that can't hold locks end to end. Break the work into steps. When one fails, run compensations for the completed ones.

The relevant lesson is that partial completion is a first-class state. A multi-agent research run that has finished three of four subtopics isn't "failed", and it isn't "succeeded". It's partially complete, and the system needs a way to represent that. Orchestration engines (BPMN, AWS Step Functions, Temporal) all grew states and error-handling branches for exactly this.

The coverage annotation in this chapter is the research-report version of a saga's completed-steps list.
2aa7ece1b9:
Part two has its own lineage. Long computations checkpoint their state so a crash doesn't lose the work: HPC jobs, database write-ahead logs, Spark lineage. Authors keep notes because working memory is small. Software teams write design docs and ADRs because the people who made a decision won't be in the room next year.

What's new with language models is that the working memory is a context window with measurable degradation. The Stanford "Lost in the Middle" paper (Liu et al., 2023) showed accuracy dropping for information placed in the middle of long inputs. Practitioner reports use the term "context rot" for the broader effect.

The remedies are the old ones. Write it down. Write it somewhere durable. Checkpoint at boundaries.
555d834a15:
Start with what a coordinator can see.

In the Claude Agent SDK, a coordinator delegates through the Task tool. It emits a tool_use block naming a subagent and a prompt. The SDK runs the subagent in its own context window. What comes back to the coordinator is the subagent's final message, delivered as a tool result. The coordinator doesn't see the subagent's tool calls, its intermediate reasoning, its exceptions or its retries.

The same holds if you build this by hand with the Messages API, with a Python function per subagent that runs its own loop. The function's return value is all the caller gets.

The channel is narrow on purpose; that's what keeps the coordinator's context small. The price is that everything the coordinator might need to know about a failure has to fit in that return value, in a form it can act on.
c0a084bbfd:
Now trace one fact, "the query timed out on the fifth call", across three designs.

  • In the swallowing design, the subagent catches the exception and returns an empty list. The coordinator receives [], and the fact is gone. A different fact replaces it: "nothing exists".
  • In the generic status design, it returns "search failed". The fact that a failure occurred survives. Its cause, its scope and the four earlier successful results don't. The coordinator's choices narrow to "believe the failure and stop" or "ignore it".
  • In the structured design, it returns the failure type, the query, the partial results and the alternatives. The coordinator has the whole decision available.

Information theory puts it bluntly: a downstream decision can be no better than the information that reaches it.
b7e96afde5:
The second principle is the one the objective calls out: the distinction between an access failure and a valid empty result.

A search tool's contract has two different zero-result situations, and their meanings are opposite. If the call succeeded and nothing matched, the empty list is information about the world ("no matching papers exist in this index"). The coordinator should treat it as a finding. If the call didn't complete, the empty list is the absence of information. The coordinator should treat it as a gap.

A design that returns [] for both leaves the coordinator unable to separate "we looked and it isn't there" from "we couldn't look". The final report built on that is wrong in exactly the places where the system was blind.
fd2dce4430: The structured payload is only useful if the categories mean something. The categories that matter are the ones that change what the next component should do. Start from the decision, not from the exception class.
9a4fba675a:
Two columns in that table carry most of the design.

The subagent column is local recovery. The objective says subagents should handle transient failures themselves and propagate only what they can't resolve. That keeps noise out of the coordinator's context: a single timeout that succeeds on retry isn't worth a sentence in the coordinator's window. It also makes the system faster to recover.

The coordinator column is the reason errors are propagated at all. Only the coordinator knows the global goal, the remaining budget, the other subagents' results and the report's required coverage. So only it can choose between "spend another call here" and "accept the gap and move on".
e404d975b8: The objective names four elements, and the surrounding material adds a fifth: the coverage statement. Each one exists because a specific decision needs it. You should be able to say which.
0a1e92bb8d: The structured payload has to survive three hops, and each hop fails in a different way. Treat them separately.
f45d386c15:
An MCP tool or custom tool reports failure to its caller with the tool result's error flag, plus content. The flag is isError in MCP and is_error on a Messages API tool_result block.

Chapter 06 covers the tool side in full. The flag says the call failed. The content is where the category, the retryable bit and the human-readable explanation go.

For this chapter, the point is that the subagent receives a failure it can classify. A tool that returns the string "Error" forces the subagent to guess. The guess then propagates upward as fact.
9b8a19e772:
This is the narrow channel from section 03. The subagent's final message is the whole payload, so the subagent's definition must say what shape that final message takes.

With the Agent SDK, the subagent is defined with an AgentDefinition (description, prompt, tools). The prompt is where you set the return contract. Put the contract there and keep the shape stable, so the coordinator's own instructions can refer to it.
53fd6334db:
The coordinator's system prompt then tells it how to act on each field. Keep this short and behavioural. An example:

"For each subagent result: put findings into the report with their sources; for each entry in failures with retryable: true and fewer than two attempts, re-delegate once with a narrower query or one of the listed alternatives; for non-retryable failures, do not retry, add the subtopic to the Coverage section; never describe a subtopic in searched_no_results as having no information, say only that the search found no matching sources."

Parameter names in the SDK change between releases. Check the docs for the current AgentDefinition fields.
5edf82c315:
The last hop is the one readers see, and it's where silent suppression does its damage. A report built from structured results can carry a coverage section. One built from flattened results can't, because the information is gone.

Section 08 builds the coverage section from the structured results. The rule is simple. Every subtopic the coordinator was asked to cover appears in the report with a coverage state, whether or not it produced findings.
40cca469a4:
Chapter 04 introduced hooks as deterministic guarantees. They help here too, as a net under the prompts.

A PostToolUse hook on the search tool can normalise heterogeneous failures into the same structured shape before the model ever sees them. (One provider's 429 body differs from another's.) Classification then doesn't depend on the model recognising three vendors' error formats.

A SubagentStop-style check on the subagent's final message verifies that it parses and contains the required keys. That lets you reject and re-ask a malformed return, instead of passing garbage upward.

Hook event names and matcher syntax are specific to the SDK version. Check the docs before relying on any of them.
9bec9cb58c: Each of these is a plausible implementation that passes a happy-path test. The broken versions are the ones the exam distractors describe. Run companion examples 01, 09 and 10 to watch them fail.
318185ebe3: The subagent recovers locally from what it can: one retry on a transient error, a reformulated query on an invalid-query error. It propagates only what it can't resolve. And it always returns partial results.
cbf7756fc0: Note the two zero-result paths. An exception leads to coverage = "none" with a failure record. An empty list leads to "searched_no_results". The coordinator and the final report treat them differently.
a2929873dd: The coordinator receives the structured result as the subagent's output and decides per failure. In the Agent SDK that output is the result of the Task tool call; in your own orchestration it's the function's return value.
5efc9ac3fc: In practice the coordinator is often the model itself, reading the structured result in its context and deciding. The same structure helps it. Given failure_type: "timeout", retried_locally: true, and alternatives, Claude will usually pick an alternative rather than repeat the same query. Given "search failed", it has nothing to reason with.
73ad32b742: The last step is honesty in the deliverable. The synthesis must say which parts are well supported, which have gaps, and why.
17146d2924: Compare "Licensing revenue: none" with "no data on licensing revenue exists". The first is accurate. The second is the silent-suppression failure, turned into a false statement.
9d3aa55411: Error paths are the least exercised code in any system. In an agent system they're also the least visible, because a model smooths over what it doesn't understand. Test them deliberately, and make them observable.
ef9277539f:
The companion's FakeSearch takes a map from query to a sequence of outcomes, consumed one per call. Each outcome is a list of hits or an exception. That's enough to express every row of the taxonomy:

  • [SearchTimeout, [hit]] is "transient, then fine";
  • [SearchForbidden] is "permanent";
  • [[]] is "valid empty".

The assertions that matter count backend calls. That's how you prove a policy rather than a hope. A 403 must produce exactly one call. A persistent timeout must produce exactly the configured number of attempts. A valid empty must produce exactly one.

Example 05 does this, and example 15 packages the checks as a unittest module for CI.
2ea24822d1:
The structured payload is for the decision-maker. The log is for the human reading it afterwards.

Per failure, log a correlation ID shared by the whole run, the subagent name, the failure type, the attempt number, the elapsed time, and the raw upstream response (truncated). If a human may need to find the log line, put only the correlation ID in the payload.

The metrics then follow from the payload for free. Count failures by type and subagent. Track the rate of not_covered subtopics per report. Alert when the share of reports with coverage gaps rises. Picture a research system whose gap rate silently doubles after a provider change. That's exactly the kind of regression that only shows up in the structured data.
e7087a5a5f:
Local retry and coordinator re-delegation both cost money and time, so bound them at both levels. A reasonable shape: each query gets at most 3 attempts, each subtopic gets at most one re-delegation, and the whole run has a wall-clock and token budget.

When the budget runs out, the coordinator proceeds and annotates. That's the objective's answer to "terminate the workflow": neither terminate nor loop, but finish with honest gaps.

Example 06 encodes the decision table. A change to the policy is then a diff to a table, not a rewrite of a prompt.
e3fc603272:
Everything above handles failures the system can see: an exception, a status code. The harder case is a tool that returns successfully with a bad answer. A search returns ten irrelevant pages. A lookup returns a stale record. A parse returns plausible but wrong fields. The system can't classify these from the transport.

What you can do is make quality visible in the payload: match scores, document dates, a count of results that passed a relevance filter. The coordinator can then apply criteria. And the validation and confidence machinery of the next chapter (task statement 5.5) catches what slips through.

State this limit plainly in the design. Structured error context fixes the failures that announce themselves.
d2a658c0ab: The exam describes the symptom: answers that mention "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes found earlier. Three mechanisms produce it, and they compound. Knowing them tells you which remedy addresses which.
530c056977:
Volume dilutes attention. Everything in the context window is available to the model, but not equally salient. A finding from hour one (OrderSubmissionService.validate() calls CreditCheckClient) sits next to hundreds of thousands of tokens of file contents, grep output and intermediate reasoning. Studies of long-context behaviour, including the "Lost in the Middle" results, show retrieval accuracy falling for material in the middle of long inputs, and models vary. The practical reading isn't a precise threshold. It's a direction: the more irrelevant text sits between a fact and the question that needs it, the less reliably the fact gets used.

Compaction generalises. When the session approaches its limit, the conversation is summarised. A summary is a compression that keeps the gist. The gist of "validate() calls CreditCheckClient wrapped by RetryingHttpAdapter with three retries and no jitter" is "validation includes a credit check with retries". The class names are the first thing to go, and the class names are what you needed.

Stale facts persist. A file read in hour one may have been edited in hour three, by you, by a teammate, or by a generator running in the same session. The old content is still in the context. The model has no automatic signal that it's out of date.
9bc18b109d:
Each remedy in the toolkit maps to a mechanism.

  • The scratchpad file defeats compaction, because the findings live on disk and survive any summary.
  • Subagent delegation defeats volume, because the verbose reads never enter the main window.
  • Phase summaries and fresh sessions defeat both volume and staleness, because the new session starts from a short, current, verified base.

A bigger context window defeats none of them. It delays the compaction, and it increases the volume.
584c001c1a:
Task 5.4 is about Claude Code sessions that run long: mapping an unfamiliar 2-million-line monolith, tracing how an order flows through 40 modules, preparing a migration plan.

Early in the session, answers are specific: "OrderSubmissionService.validate() in order-core calls CreditCheckClient through RetryingHttpAdapter." Several hours and many file reads later, answers drift: "the service layer typically validates the order before calling downstream clients."

The model is now describing typical Spring applications, not this one. Its answers become inconsistent with earlier ones.
0f4d1f2fbd:
The mechanism is the same one as in Chapter 14. Every Read, Grep and Bash output is appended to context. The specific findings from hour one now sit in the middle of a very long context, surrounded by file contents that were relevant once.

Then the context is compacted, either automatically near the limit or with /compact. Those findings get summarised along with everything else, and specific class names are exactly what a summary generalises.
206f3d6da0:
The "how you confirmed it" column matters. It lets a later session, or a reviewer, tell a verified finding from an inference.

It also ties into task 2.5 (Chapter 07). You trace usage through wrapper modules like LegacyOrderFacade with Grep, then read the files that matter. That's how you build understanding step by step instead of reading the whole tree.
8db6f1aeaa:
Say the terminal closes, or the session is too polluted to trust. A new session starts with: "Read docs/exploration/state.json and NOTES.md, then continue with the first pending item."

That's often more reliable than resuming the old session. The old context holds file contents that may have changed since they were read (task 1.7).
7d59da4740: A custom read-only subagent for discovery keeps the main session clean. In Claude Code, subagent definitions live in .claude/agents/ as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter:
ad7ab902aa:
The main session then asks: "Use the code-mapper agent to find every caller of LegacyOrderFacade and what each one passes." The subagent may read 40 files, while the main context grows by 25 lines.

The subagent starts with no history (task 1.2). So the request must contain everything it needs: the question, the module names, and any findings it should build on.
be2d7ee46c:
/compact summarises the conversation to free context. It accepts optional instructions about what to keep, for example /compact keep all file paths, class names and open questions; drop file contents.

Two rules apply. Write findings to the scratchpad before compacting, so nothing depends on the summary. And compact at phase boundaries, not in the middle of tracing a call chain.
ace870b9ba: If your subagent tools front existing Spring services, the structured context often starts life as a Java exception mapped in a controller advice. The point is that the classification happens once, at the edge that knows the cause. From there it travels as data, not as a message string.
e3ce566a31: The MCP wrapper (Chapter 06) then returns this body with isError: true. The subagent passes it upward with its own partial results added. Nobody along the chain converts it to a string.
3e22261d49:
Structured doesn't mean verbose. A coordinator that receives full stack traces and raw HTTP bodies from five subagents has a context problem (Chapter 14).

Keep the error payload to the fields that change a decision: type, retryable, attempted operation, partial results, alternatives, coverage. Log the stack trace in your own observability system with a correlation ID. If humans need to trace it later, put only that ID in the payload.
e4943687ee: Large-codebase exploration also needs an end condition, or sessions grow until they degrade. Use the question as the boundary, not the codebase:
eb9f545d0e:
Delegating and writing things down only help if the exploration itself is efficient. Two million lines can't be read. They have to be searched.

The objective's companion task statement (2.5, Chapter 07) names the tools: Grep for content, Glob for paths, Read for whole files, Edit for targeted changes. The strategy that follows from those tools is a funnel.
1261098381:
Start where control enters the system: controllers, message listeners, scheduled jobs, main methods. Record each entry point in the scratchpad.

Then trace one flow end to end before broadening. A traced flow gives you the vocabulary, meaning the real class names and the real layering, that makes later searches precise. A search for CreditCheckClient is cheap and exact. A search for "credit check" is neither.
37c487e453:
Enterprise code is full of facades, adapters and legacy shims. Finding the definition of a function tells you little if forty callers go through LegacyOrderFacade.

The method:

  1. Grep for the class name with a trailing dot or paren to find callers.
  2. Group the callers by module.
  3. Read one representative of each group.
  4. Write down the call chain, including the wrapper.

Chapter 07 covers the tool semantics. The new element here is that each step's result goes into NOTES.md as soon as it's confirmed.
1eef21ae90:
The scratchpad is only as reliable as its entries. Every entry should carry the path, the symbol and how it was confirmed.

Example 11 shows the cheap check this enables. A script takes each entry and tests that the path exists and the symbol appears in the file. That catches both hallucinated entries and stale ones left after refactors. For a team, run it in CI against the notes of a long-lived migration effort.
62862133d3:
You can test whether a session has degraded. Keep five or six "probe questions" whose answers are specific symbols recorded in NOTES.md. Ask them after a compaction, or at the start of a resumed session.

If the answers name the symbols, the session is healthy. If they say "typically", start fresh from the file.

Example 13 simulates the pattern with clearly labelled invented numbers. A real probe uses your own repository.
6a14a1f1b2:
The last remedy is borrowed from long-running batch jobs. Assume the process will be interrupted, and make the work resumable.

A Claude Code session can be interrupted by a closed terminal, a crash, a context that has become unusable, or a colleague taking over. If the only copy of the progress is in the conversation, the progress is gone.
8e44dbe03c:
Two details make this work in practice.

First, write the file atomically. Write to a temporary file and rename it. A crash mid-write then can't leave a half-written state.json that the next session can't parse (example 12).

Second, put in the state file the information a stranger needs: the task statement, the phase list, what's done, what's pending, which files matter, and where the notes live. The test: open the file as someone who has never seen the session, and ask whether they could continue.
ed74784f7a:
Chapter 04 (task 1.7) covers --resume and fork_session. For long exploration, the decision rule is this:

  • Resume when the context is still healthy and nothing it relies on has changed.
  • Restart from the state file when the session shows degradation symptoms, when many tool results have gone stale, or when the work is being handed to someone else.

A restart costs one short prompt ("Read state.json and NOTES.md; continue with the first pending item"). It buys a clean, verified base.
91ee75e963: Answer: C. A is silent suppression, and it produces a false "nothing exists". B keeps the fact of failure but loses everything the coordinator needs to recover. D throws away partial work from the other subagents. C is the only option that supports a recovery decision.
102da8b743: Answer: B. The valid empty result and the access failure need different representations: empty success versus an error flag with a category. D is backwards. Retrying a true empty result wastes calls and may loop.
270246e43e: Answer: B. The specifics decayed under volume and compaction. A delays the problem and increases volume. C makes the generalisation happen more often. D has no mechanism. The file survives compaction, and the subagent keeps the volume out of the main window.
fbebdef3ef: Answer: B. The objective calls for coverage annotations. A hides the gap. C fabricates coverage. D throws away six good topics.
843c61ee77: Answer: B. It makes the worst case "redo one phase". Scrollback is unstructured, and it carries the same stale tool output. A and D don't address loss at all.
e1a4b8b62e: Implement run_queries from section 08 with a mock search. It should time out on one subtopic (twice), return [] on another, raise 403 on a third, and return hits on the fourth.
a9a52986ed: Done when: the structured version reports four different coverage states correctly. The 403 is never retried. The timeout is retried locally exactly the configured number of times. And the silent version demonstrably states something false. Companion examples 01, 05 and 07 are the reference.
03bd74a4a1: Done when: after compaction and in the fresh session, answers name the same files and symbols as phase 1, with no "typically" phrasing. The main session context never held the raw content of more than a handful of files. Run example 11's verifier against your notes.
